record.paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings
record.original_question: Suppose a cubic graph admits a 2-homogeneous coloring, meaning a proper vertex-coloring in which exactly 2 colors appear in the open neighborhood of every vertex. Is it always possible to find such a coloring using only 4 colors?

evidence.quote:
A proper coloring of vertices where in the open neighborhood of every vertex exactly k colors
appear is k-homogeneous coloring [1]. ... Problem 5.1 If a cubic graph admits a 2-homogeneous coloring, then 4 colors are always
sufficient.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G be a cubic graph (a simple graph in which every vertex has degree exactly 3). A proper vertex coloring of G is an assignment of colors to the vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors. For a positive integer k, such a coloring is called k-homogeneous if, for every vertex v of G, exactly k distinct colors appear among the vertices in the open neighborhood N(v) of v (i.e., among the three neighbors of v, ignoring v itself).

Prove or disprove: every cubic graph G that admits a 2-homogeneous proper vertex coloring also admits a 2-homogeneous proper vertex coloring that uses at most 4 colors.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search for "2-homogeneous coloring" of cubic graphs did not return any published resolution; the question appears as a posed open problem and no proof or counterexample could be located.

status_evidence.title: Graph coloring - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: General overview of graph coloring variants; no mention of resolved 2-homogeneous coloring of cubic graphs.
status_evidence.claim: No standard reference reports a resolution of the 4-color sufficiency for 2-homogeneous colorings of cubic graphs.

status_evidence.title: Coloring with no 2-colored P4's (Albertson et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses related restricted coloring concepts but does not address 2-homogeneous colorings of cubic graphs.
status_evidence.claim: Closely related literature on restricted colorings does not contain a resolution of this specific problem.
